analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 income tax rate cuts permanent instead of expiring after 2010.
analysis.headline: The bill got 21 Republican cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Ways and Means Committee when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law (EGTRRA) cut income tax rates across the board, with the largest dollar benefits going to the highest earners. Because of Senate budget rules, the cuts were written to expire after 2010 — the bill text itself amends that expiration provision. H.R. 2212 would have struck the expiration date and made the rate cuts permanent. It was introduced in June 2001, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and was never taken up before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers in higher brackets gain the most, since the 2001 rate cuts cut the top rates by the largest margins and high earners pay income tax at those rates on most of their income. Making the cuts permanent also removed the risk that they would lapse, which mattered most to people with the largest tax bills.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently extends the individual income tax rate reductions enacted in the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, which would otherwise sunset after 2010 under that law's own terms.
The bill amends section 901 of EGTRRA so that the rate cuts in section 101 continue 'without regard to' the sunset provisions in subsections (a) and (b).

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost: permanently forgoing the revenue that the scheduled expiration was designed to recapture. That revenue shortfall must be covered by borrowing, by future tax increases, or by cuts to government programs; the burden falls on future taxpayers and on whatever spending gets squeezed.

drawbacks.text: The expiration date in EGTRRA was a budget-rule device: the cuts were phased over ten years so they would fit within reconciliation limits, meaning permanence converts a temporary, deficit-managed measure into a permanent revenue reduction.

The rate cuts' benefits were concentrated at the top of the income scale, so permanence mainly locks in savings for the highest earners while adding to long-term deficits that pressure future spending on programs ordinary people rely on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ordinary taxpayers did get some relief from the 2001 rate cuts, so permanence was not worthless to them. But the largest and most durable gains went to households in the top brackets, and the cost — a permanent hole in federal revenue — falls diffuse and deferred, on deficits and future budget choices. As drafted, the bill addressed only the rate cuts and nothing about offsetting the revenue loss.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Tiberi introduced the bill on June 19, 2001, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — between the referral and the end of the Congress on January 3, 2003.
The bill drew 21 cosponsors, all of them House Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: the scheduled 2010 expiration on the rate cuts stayed on the books through this Congress, preserving the option of letting them lapse and the revenue attached to that. The high earners who stood to gain the most from permanence saw this effort fail, though separate legislation later in the decade took up similar questions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury and the scheduled sunset

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Tiberi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 rate cuts permanent and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 21 cosponsors were Republicans; there is no record of any Democratic cosponsor or of any floor action where a partisan split could have shown up.

industries.note: The 2001 rate cuts trimmed the top rates the most, so making them permanent delivers the biggest, most durable savings to the highest earners. Their gain is the federal revenue the expiration was designed to recapture.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax planning industry
industries.note: A permanent rate schedule would simplify long-term planning modestly, but the industry had already absorbed the 2001 cuts; the marginal effect of this bill alone was small.
